I do not know how listing the Scarlet Macaw on the ESA List is going to benefit the Wild Populations. These birds are not on the endangered list in their Native Countries. Scarlet Macaws have not been imported into the United States in 20+ years. Adding these birds to this list is not going to help the wild population but it will make ownership in the State illegal, which means that many people who have these birds in their homes as beloved pets automatically become law breaking citizens over night. If this bill is passed it hurts the "Pet Owner" as well as the Beloved Pets people have in their homes. There is no benefit from adding the Scarlet Macaw or any other non native parrot species to said list. If anything you are inciting a death sentence to all domesticated Scarlet Macaws in the State.

Marine life in New York has always been important to me. I attend the Harbor School on Governors Island because of my interest in protecting our ecosystem. In addition, I am also a scuba diver who has spent days underwater, surrounded by countless number of fish. I am in support of these regulations as it is important to protect the Summer Flounder, Scup, Black Sea Bass, and Bluefish. Putting limits on these species allows for long-term sustainability in the north-east waters. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, they state, “The number of overfished stocks globally has tripled in half a century, and today fully one-third of the world's assessed fisheries are currently pushed beyond their biological limits.” This regulation, though a small step in the entire issue, moves to help this ongoing problem. In addition, National Geographic claims “Fishers remove more than 77 billion kilograms (170 billion pounds) of wildlife from the sea each year. Scientists fear that continuing to fish at this rate may soon result in a collapse of the world’s fisheries. To continue relying on the ocean as an important food source, economists and conservationists say we will need to employ sustainable fishing practices.” It is important for the rule to be implemented for the protection of the listed species. Regulations such as this one should be expanded to more species to protect the overall health of our environment. For example, the shortnose sturgeon is currently endangered according to the New York Department of Environmental Conservation. Rules should be expanded to include more species for increased biodiversity within our habitats. Therefore, this regulation has my full support for being passed, but more species of fish that are being harmed by overfishing should be included in regulations such as these. Long-term sustainability should be a goal that everyone reaches for, and small steps like this continue to push us in the right direction.

September 02, 2025 
 
 
The United Steelworkers (USW), is one of the largest industrial unions in North America 
and a voice for approximately 20,000 miners in the United States and an equivalent 
number in Canada. Our members work in underground and surface mines and quarries, 
utilizing various mining methods and equipment to extract almost every commodity, the 
exception is coal. 
 
USW strongly opposes the Mine Safety and Health Administration’s (MSHA) proposed 
revision to 30 CFR Part 48 that seeks to eliminate provisions allowing District Managers 
to require changes or additions to training programs. While the agency frames this 
revision as a matter of statutory alignment and procedural propriety, such a move is 
detrimental to the health and safety of miners that will potentially lead to more injuries, 
illnesses and fatalities. Stripping District Managers of the ability to intervene, update, or 
require specific training modifications ignores the dynamic and hazardous nature of 
mining operations and reduces MSHA’s capacity to respond swiftly to emerging risks. 
USW believes this proposal would undermine hard-won protections, lower training 
standards, and expose miners to preventable injury and death. 
 
First and foremost, the mining environment is not static. New hazards emerge daily from 
changes in geological conditions, equipment design, operational methods, or unforeseen 
events such as roof falls, chemical exposures, or technological malfunctions. Training 
programs, if locked into rigid, nationally uniform templates, will inevitably lag behind the 
evolving realities miners face. Currently, District Managers play a crucial role in bridging 
that gap by requiring adjustments to site-specific training programs when hazards are 
discovered or when accident data reveals deficiencies. Removing this authority assumes 
that a one-size-fits-all training approach can anticipate every hazard across diverse mines 
and regions. That assumption is not only unrealistic, but also reckless. The iron ore miner 
in Minnesota navigating complex mining machinery and the stone miner in the Midwest 
exposed to silica dust each face unique risks. A regulatory framework that prohibits local 
officials from tailoring training to these conditions would condemn miners to a system 
where safety training is always playing catch-up. In essence, MSHA’s proposal elevates 
legal formalism over the lived realities of working miners.

 
Second, USW rejects the assertion that District Managers’ current authority violates the 
Appointments Clause or the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). District Managers are 
career professionals within MSHA who possess technical expertise and firsthand 
knowledge of mining conditions. Their authority to require modifications in training is not 
the exercise of “significant regulatory power” in the constitutional sense, but rather a 
necessary administrative function delegated to ensure the statutory mandate of the 
Federal Mine Safety and Health Act of 1977 is fulfilled: to protect miners’ lives. Congress 
expressly designed the Mine Act to be preventative and adaptive, recognizing the need 
for regulators to address hazards proactively rather than reactively. District Managers’ 
ability to order training adjustments is consistent with this preventative purpose.

I have fished recreationally for Black Sea Bass on charter vessels off of CT and Cape Cod for over 30 years and have a degree in Marine Biology. Importantly, you have acknowledged that the Northeast stock is in good shape (not surprisingly since the species is increasing in the northeast with warmer waters)
My comment is simple- get rid of the minimum size limits and use the ( certainly low) bag limits to achieve Conservation Equivalency. As you know, most of the fish are caught with cut bait (e.g. squid strips) from depths often exceeding 50 feet. It makes NO SENSE to lose, for example, perfectly edible 14” fish ( a limit I’m old enough to remember), or for that matter any smaller fish with even less reproductive potential. Your stock biomass objectives are readily achievable by bag limits. Please encourage this change in your interaction with the states.

I HIGHLY support the proposed critical habitat protections for the five threatened Caribbean coral species and seven threatened Indo-Pacific coral species. All of these species have undergone population decline and are highly susceptible to multiple threats. The most severe threats are attributed to climate change which NMFS describes as creating a foreseeable likelihood and danger of extinction for these corals throughout all of their ranges. 

An estimated 50% of coral reefs worldwide have already been lost to climate change, and about one-third of reef-building coral species are at risk of extinction. Stressors and risks to threatened coral species include both climate related threats as well as ecological effects of fishing and land-based sources of pollution. Severe impacts of the climate crisis include ocean acidification, which hinders the ability of corals to grow, and ocean warming, which causes coral bleaching. 

Critical habitat designations are necessary to reduce and remove threats to healthy ocean conditions which foster growth and recovery of these threatened species. Coral reefs help support over 25% of all marine life, and designation of critical habitat for these coral species means a chance for recovery and the opportunity to save them from extinction. THANK YOU for your commitment to saving these corals, and the critical habitat and the enormous diverse ecosystems that they support.

The Hawaiian Hawk should not be removed from the List of Endangered and Threatened Wildlife under the Endangered Species Act. There has not been enough improvement in the hawks vulnerable habitat, and increases in urban and subdivision development leave the hawks habitat even more vulnerable to decreases in size. 
 The Hawaiian Hawk is Hawaiis only hawk, and only breeds on the Big Island (American Bird Conservancy). They have a very limited range and require native forests for their survival, because they will only breed and nest in native trees (Honolulu Zoo Society). The species will suffer if delisted because there is still a decline in the amount of native forest in Hawaii, and the forests used for nesting and breeding are vulnerable to invasive species, like the strawberry guava, which is detrimental to the survival of the Hawaiian Hawk. The trees used by the hawk for nesting are also vulnerable to dieback caused by ROD, which is also detrimental to the survival of the hawk. The already limited area of natural habitat and the decrease in habitat means that this species should not be delisted or it may not survive.

 Subpart A Section 296.4 The definition of Household should be modified to clarify that it does not exclude the claims of owners that did not live at the property on a continuous basis. 

Subpart A Section 296.4 Household excludes extended family members that did not live at the property. They should be included in Household; but not compensated for financial damages already paid to primary resident. Extended family members should be eligible for compensation based on their individual loss. 

Subpart B Section 296.14 Assignment of the proceeds of the claim is not allowed. It should certainly be allowed in death. If the claim is legitimate, the owner’s right to assign for a variety of valid reasons should not be limited. 

Subpart C 296.21 (a) Allowable damages should be expanded to include non-economic damages. Loss of enjoyment and loss of lifestyle are real and significant; thus, should be included. Loss of wildlife is a true loss. Mental and emotional distress and sentimental losses should also be covered. Also include disturbance and annoyance damages. All damages and all losses should be covered. For many, these are greater and more important than the financial loss. 

Subpart C 296.21(a) Requires actual damages to be reasonable. It should be changed to actual damages supported. 

Subpart C 296.21(a) Expand to include compensation for lost sentimental value for damaged real and personal property based on Castillo v. City of Las Vegas, 195 P.3d 870, 875 (N.M. Ct. App. 2008). 

Subpart C Section 296.21(b) Excludes reimbursement for attorney’s fees and agents’ fees, plus claimant’s cost of prosecuting a claim. These should be reimbursed.

Take nitrates out of organic meat
The Organic Foods Production Act (OFPA) prohibits the addition of nitrates to organic food because of the known health effects, but producers of organic processed meat products, along with producers of nonorganic nitrate free meats, have found a way around that prohibition celery powder. The high levels of nitrate fertilizer allowed in nonorganic production concentrate in some vegetables, including celery, but organically grown celery does not contain high enough levels of nitrate to be used in curing meat. Celery powder has been listed as an allowed nonorganic agricultural ingredient since 2007.

Nitrates are prohibited in organic food because of their impacts on human health, which include methemoglobinemia, hypotension, risk of pregnancy complications, a number of reproductive effects, and cancer. In addition, the Beyond Pesticides Eating with a Conscience database identifies impacts of pesticides used in producing nonorganic celery, including farmworker poisonings, contamination of water, wildlife poisoning, and pollinator impacts. The NOSB must deny the relisting of celery powder.

I am a Professor in the Department of Zoology at the University of Otago, an elected Fellow of the 

Royal Society of New Zealand, and a member of the IUCN (World Conservation Union) Conservation 

Translocation Specialist Group (CTSG), in which capacity I was head of the CTSG Bird Section for 10 

years. I am a co-author of the IUCN’s 2013 Reintroduction Guidelines, and have participated in and 

advised on species reintroduction projects in New Zealand, Australia, Europe, North America, and the 

Middle East, over the last 30 years. 

I have reviewed the Proposed rule to establish an experimental population of sihek on Palmyra Atoll as 

part of ongoing efforts for the conservation of this critically endangered species, and in the following I 

offer my comments, and my strong support, for this important project. 

The sihek (Guam kingfisher, Todiramphus cinnamominus) is as endangered as a bird species can get, 

officially designated as “Extinct in the Wild” following its extirpation, largely as a result of predation 

by invasive brown tree snake, from Guam some 30 years ago. Sihek are island endemics, once found 

nowhere else apart from the island of Guam, but now reduced to some 150 individuals across fewer 

than 30 AZA institutions. Captive populations cannot be maintained indefinitely without inadvertent 

selection for undesirable traits, so while the sihek studbook management has worked to sustain genetic 

and demographic health of the captive populations, there is a slow decline in total population size and 

increasing risk of inbreeding depression that could compromise future restoration efforts. There is 

some urgency therefore, to enhance population size and diversity. 

At present sihek habitat on Guam is compromised by the continued presence of brown tree snakes. 

Under the IUCN CTSG Guidelines, reintroductions should not take place until the original cause of 

extirpation has been addressed, therefore release of sihek back onto Guam is not currently possible. 

Nevertheless, good progress is being made towards the eventual eradication of brown tree snake so the 

future restoration of sihek to Guam remains a goal. However, any reintroduction is a complex process 

carrying a risk of failure. The development of the science of reintroduction biology over the last 20 

years has indicated that reintroduction success can be markedly improved through the development of 

species-specific translocation procedures that refine the stages of transport, release, and post-release 

monitoring and care. The very best way to develop and refine translocation procedures is through 

experimental releases to create trial populations where management options to enhance survival rates, 

productivity, and population persistence can be tested and compared. The current proposal aims to do 

just that through the creation of an experimental population of sihek. 

 Sihek is endemic to Guam and with Guam unsuitable currently for sihek reintroduction it is necessary 

to consider creation of an experimental population through translocation outside the indigenous range.

Background 
 
 
NMFS is proposing to issue permits pursuant to section 101(a)(5)(E) of the Marine Mammal 
Protection Act (MMPA) to allow the unintentional mortality or serious injury (M/SI) of marine 
mammals belonging to five populations listed as or proposed for listing as endangered or threatened 
under the Endangered Species Act. The taking would be incidental to three BSAI groundfish 
fisheries (i.e., trawl fisheries for flatfish and pollock, and a longline fishery for Pacific cod). The five 
affected marine mammal populations are endangered western and central North Pacific humpback 
whales, endangered western Steller sea lions, threatened Alaska ringed seals, and Alaska bearded 
seals, which have been proposed for listing as threatened. Such incidental take permits can be issued 
if, in part, NMFS determines that expected incidental M/SI is likely to have a negligible impact on 
the affected marine mammal stocks. 
 
 
In 1999, NMFS adopted five criteria for making negligible impact determinations (NIDs) 
when considering the effects of commercial fishing on endangered and threatened marine mammal 
populations. For the three BSAI groundfish fisheries included in the proposed action, the notice 
states that NMFS has reached a preliminary conclusion that permits are warranted for all five marine 
mammal populations based on two of the five criteria established for making NIDs. The two

3 the total annual fishery-related M/SI is between 10-100% of PBR and the population

division of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Organization (NOAA), under the authority of

We support the proposed CTTP, apart from some aspects of the third-party auditing 
process and proposed repercussions for noncompliance. The CTTP requires an annual audit, 
giving the importer discretion to initiate the process and to designate a neutral third party to 
conduct the audit. The annual audit requirement is an essential procedure in which the NMFS 
can ensure the importer is remaining in compliance with its Trusted Trader Compliance Plan. In 
fact, the importer’s adherence to the audit requirements and production of the audit report to the 
NMFS are the only mandatory safeguards against CTTP noncompliance. In addition, if the 
importer fails to provide the audit report as required by the CTTP or fails to take acceptable 
corrective actions, the NMFS may revoke the importer's “CTT status.”

This letter is in response to the proposed rule change by the Federal Aviation Administration concerning The Medical Certification Standards for Commercial Balloon Operations. I am writing this response to proposed rule change, in hopes that the FAA will consider all testimonies being made about the proposed rule change, and will not put the Rule Change in to effect as written.
Commercial Hot Air Balloon operations take in so many different facets that need to be considered. Commercial Hot Air Balloon Pilots have the Commercial rating for many different reasons. There are pilots, that fly Corporate balloons, perform tethered operations for events, fly special shapes, fly corporate banners and advertising, train new pilots, preform biannual flight check rides for other pilots, attend organized events around the country and fly passengers for the event organizers, operate small businesses providing occasional Hot Air Balloon Flights, for 3-6 passengers. and then you have the pilots that fly large balloons that can carry more than six passengers up to 20 passengers.
​History shows that the majority of Hot Air Balloon incidents and accidents, occur from the large ride balloon (8 or more passengers), and not so much from the smaller activities that require a commercial license.
If the proposed Standards for Rule Change is actually imposed as written, it will have far over reaching consequences, for other industries that are part of the aviation industry. This proposed change will not only effect more than 3000 pilots that currently hold a commercial pilot license for Hot Air Balloons, but it will also have an effect, on, Flight Training schools, repair stations, insurance companies, and even affect the decision of future people thinking about becoming a licensed Hot Air Balloon Pilot.
This proposed change in the Standards requiring a Second Class Medical Statement across the board of all pilots that hold commercial licenses, it will also create a logistics night mare for the FAA itself. The tracking and oversight of such a regulation will further overburden the FAA system. 
At the present time there is a very small amount of Doctors that are certified to do a 2nd class medical. With the passage of tis new standard, even the doctors that are approved by the FAA to preform these medical exams will be over burdened, The time frame of 180 days for compliance to obtain the 2nd class medical is not enough time. This time frame if implemented should be atleast one year, to allow all persons involved, time to comply. 
With the limited amount of Pilots that carry a commercial Hot Air Balloon License, that are currently training new pilots, the growth in the industry will come to a near standstill, if commercial pilots are forced to obtain a 2nd class medical exam. Most new pilots come from being part of a Hot Air Balloon team, and decide to work with their pilots to obtain their own pilots license. If the commercial pilot is unable to teach or continue their small business, because of a mandatory rule change, the Hot Air Balloon Aviation industry will slowly become a thing of the past.
In final thoughts, I urge the committee to table this proposal in order to consider all the ramifications of the change. I further urge the committee that if they do go forward, to do it in three phases. First only Balloon Pilots that fly large balloons that can carry 8 or more passengers be required to obtain the 2nd class medical exam. The second phase would be to add more FAA personnel that are trained in the operations of Hot Air Balloons, including adding more DPE Flight examiners. The third phase would be after one year to put together a realistic 3-5 year program, and then revisit the proposed rule change, and look at the historic data, to see if the change is actually necessary. 
Please Please listen to the leaders in our industry concerning Hot Air Balloons, especially the Balloon Federation of America (BFA), before any changes are made.

These comments primarily respond to comments submitted by GE Avionics.

The optics of enabling supersonic flights over land are not good. While supersonic flight might create new possibilities for how people travel and experience the world around us, these luxuries are likely to be limited in practice to the top 0.1% of Americans given that supersonic travel uses far more fuel (3 times for a Concorde) than subsonic travel and will be much more expensive. If carbon conservation is really the goal, the solution is not to drive down the cost of a ticket through more efficient use of carbon fuels, increasing demand for a highly inefficient mode of travel, it is to have fewer inefficient flights. When the benefit of an hour less travel time coast-to-coast for the top 0.1% is set against hundreds of thousands of people being exposed to a sonic boom with each such flight, we have a marquee issue for those who question just who government is serving.

Toward this end, the manufacture and production of supersonic aircraft should be subject to the same standards as the manufacture and production of subsonic aircraft. This includes the Part 36 Stage criteria, which are important for controlling noise below ~8000 near airports, regardless of whether the aircraft is used for supersonic flight. Metroplexes have been heavily impacted by NextGen. Reverting to Stage 3 criteria established in 1977 for aircraft to be manufactured in the 2020s, as GE Avionics suggests with their language that supersonic aircraft... be no louder than aircraft operating around our airports today, would make a mockery of the promise - certainly implied if not explicit - that the Stage criteria represent a rising bar that is designed to protect residents from noise as time moves on.

The suggestion of GE Avionics that the no measurable sonic boom overpressure language be replaced with a test of no significant impact might make sense in a world where impacts that really are significant are effectively measured and controlled. Sadly, we do not live in such a world, as residents across the United States, many members of Congress and the Senate and, I think, even the FAA must acknowledge since the introduction of NextGen. The 65 DNL standard does not correlate well with annoyance for several reasons: Many people outside the 65dB contours are highly annoyed and have spent tens of thousands of dollars on window upgrades without reimbursement, as I have, or are considering moving. 65 DNL heavily discounts the frequencies that are most likely to penetrate walls and windows through its reliance on dB-A weighted metrics, rather than dB-C, frequencies for which people have little tolerance. It does not consider the frequency of noise events, because it does not discriminate between many noisy incidents and fewer louder ones.
